utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I appear for the Prosecution with Mr. Scott, Mr. Lopez-Terres, and we are also joined today by Mr. Harmon because the binding order litigation was so closely integrated with the binding order litigation that started in the Blaskic case, which he prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. For the Federation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Amir Ahmic, a liaison officer for the International Tribunal in The Hague here is one of those appearing for Bosnia, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I'm Ivan Tomic, lawyer, and I am substituting today for temporarily-absent Robert Muselimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. There is before the Court this afternoon applications, as I understand it, relating to a number of matters; first of all, the non-compliance, as alleged, with orders made by the Trial Chamber on the 4th of February and the 1st of June of last year, and an application relating to a request made on the 19th of July. We have had before us material which we've recently received, dated the 10th of January from Mr. Tomic and the 12th of January from Mr. Ahmic. We also have Prosecution application and submissions dated the 22nd of December. It may be convenient for the Prosecution to start, to tell us at the outset what they are asking us to do, and then we'll hear submissions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll introduce matters, but briefly, because Mr. Scott has dealt with the detail. First of all, I recall that we haven't seen any authority supporting Mr. Tomic's substitution for Mr. Muselimovic. We knew of his authority. That may be of some significance when I take you to one matter of detail a little later. In summary, we seek various orders. Mr. Scott will deal with that in more detail. Our basic premise is that there has been non-compliance, intentional; that orders made should now be very short in terms of time allowed; and that the Chamber should supervise actively the production of any documents, that is to say -- I'm asked to check whether we're in open or closed session. As I understand it, we are in open session and there's no challenge to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to our being in open session? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I return to what we seek; namely, that the Chamber should supervise actively the production of any documents, asking them to be produced to the Chamber, following such return dates perhaps almost immediately or very, very shortly afterwards by return dates as the individuals to address the question whether production has been sufficient or not. The alternative to such a process, as we can see from the schedule produced by Mr. Scott, is that very substantial delays get built in. Indeed, I think it's worth noting that in the absence of timetabled return dates, the application for a hearing made on the 22nd of June was outstanding until today's date, so time passes very quickly, and that's a very compelling reason for the Chamber to take a grip of these matters, it may think, and supervise them itself. I'm also going to respectfully suggest that the representatives of the parties could take account of the fact that although the Chamber is incompletely composed today, there being only two Judges, not three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's my omission. The position is this: that Judge Robinson is away for urgent personal reasons, as I hope the parties have been informed. We cannot make any orders in his absence, as a Trial Chamber. Unless there is any objection, in order to save time and to expedite matters, we propose to hear oral argument now, and then when we are composed as a Trial Chamber, we will make orders arising from it. Judge Robinson can, of course, read the transcript of this hearing and join in any decision. He will be returning on or about the 25th of January. Is there any objection to our following that course? There is an indication that there is none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I return to where I was, then. I'm going respectfully to suggest that the representatives of the parties can take account of the fact that some time will pass between today and Judge Robinson's return and thus between today and the first moment when any order can be made, and that they could and should take steps to prepare documentation for compliance with orders, and that the time allowed thereafter in the orders of the Chamber, if any such orders are made, should take account of the ability of the parties to use the intervening time to prepare themselves. That said, I have two other points to make. In light of the closeness of the Bosnian Croat side of the Federation with Croatia itself and the Defence of Kordic, non-compliance or failure to produce documents will, in our submission, in due course run the risk of adverse inferences properly being inferred or drawn, contrary to the interests of Kordic, and it's important that those representing that part of the Federation should know that. The last point I want to deal with is dealt with at page 35 of the brief drafted by Mr. Scott. It is the passage that deals with the meetings between various parties concerning the Kordic Defence, a meeting that in our submission fits with what will or may already have been inferred about purposes of obstruction being found in part of the Federation. I'm able to tell the Chamber this, and happy to do so, that the documents upon which the Prosecution rely were seized shortly before Christmas by NATO; nothing to do with the OTP. They were seized in Mostar. They were seized because NATO was concerned about non-compliance with the Dayton Agreement. The documents were seized in one building masquerading as another, and of course the disguising of the purposes of buildings is one of the general problems we may face. The documents seized appear, in general, to show a connection between Croatia intelligence and work being done contrary to the Dayton Agreement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, some of those documents have been made available to us, and it's those documents upon which we rely, and the Chamber will already have noted that there is no challenge to any of the detail so far, no challenge to any of the details recited. At page 35, the Chamber may wish to understand the degree to which those documents, as summarised, implicate the Croat part of the Federation. On page 35, summarising the effect of the first substantial document, we see that present at the meeting, (d), was Primorac, the overall head of the Bosnian Croat Secret Service, and -- and here comes an interesting fact -- (e), Robert Muselimovic, the accredited liaison officer now to this institution and the man expected to appear here today. The principal document that was relied on was drafted by the man Muselimovic. And as a matter of interest, the second document that is referred to -- and you'll see that at paragraph 79, at the foot of page 36 -- was addressed to Ante Jelavic, a name that the Chamber will find set out on the first page of the schedule that Mr. Scott's prepared. He, at the time that the schedule refers to him, being the Minister to whom Judge McDonald issued an order for compliance, an order which was never respected and complied with. So that's the way in which those recently discovered matters involve and implicate the Croatian part of the Federation. I'll hand over to Mr. Scott for the detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, representatives of the Federation. Your Honour, I'm sure the Court's heard more of me today than you probably would like, so I'll try to be short, partly because I think this proceeding is postured differently than the one we had this morning in this respect: The Court has already come to grips, to some extent, with the non-compliance of the Federation with at least one of the outstanding orders, and that is the order of this Court dated the 4th of February of 1999. There was a compliance hearing, if you will, on that on the 20th May of last year, in which the Court made a finding of non-compliance, followed by a written order on the 1st of June, again documenting non-compliance and ordering certain follow-up, if you will, by the Federation, including the identification of senior -- specific senior officials to make a further response to the Court essentially as to why there had not been compliance. In that sense, Your Honour, we are postured a little further along perhaps in this proceeding than in the earlier proceeding today. Having said that, let me touch upon -- I'm going to use, I think, this afternoon a bit more than I did this morning the table which I understand has been provided to the representatives for the Federation, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got this table?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I will do, Your Honour, is move through some of these events and stop at some places to add a little bit more information out of our submission of December 22nd. I will say again that that submission, we believe, is quite detailed, quite exhaustive in many respects, and can say more fully what I can probably say on my feet this afternoon, and we certainly rely on the full submission. In terms of the table or summary, we, again, Your Honour, face this afternoon a situation which takes us back and runs a history of some three years. On the 15th of January, 1997, starting with box number 3 or item 3 on the chart, Judge McDonald, at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor in the Blaskic case issued a subpoena to the Federation. That then, if you will, initiated a series of orders, further subpoenas, findings, all directed to the Federation throughout essentially the remainder of calendar year 1997. As the table notes, for instance at item 12 -- but I'll tell the Court again this is not a full -- by any means a completely detailed account, because if we were to include every order and every piece of correspondence, the summary would be even quite a bit longer than it is. Suffice it to say for today's purposes that starting with item number 3 and continuing through item number 8, there were a series of continuing orders and subpoenas from Judge McDonald, trying to obtain compliance with the subpoena. The subpoena, Your Honours, asked for many of the same documents that we continue to seek today. So we again find ourselves in a position of now having spent some three years seeking these documents. I will just note in particular, Judge McDonald, as early as the 28th of February, 1997, in item 5, even at that early date reached the point of issuing a show-cause order which then Minister of Defence Jelavic should not be held in contempt. As Mr. Nice has already indicated, just to show how intertwined, some might say incestuous, the story is, this is the same Mr. Jelavic who, as we speak, is the president, the chairman of the Federation, of the presidency of the Federation. That position, as the Court may know, rotates between the Bosniak member of the presidency, the Serbian -- the Bosnian Serbian member of the presidency and the Bosnian Muslim member of the presidency, and since approximately June of last year, this same Mr. Jelavic is the president. That ultimately led to -- that ultimately led to -- to finish on 1997, and is further again detailed in our briefs, which is again -- there's a much longer story to this. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Leading to an exchange of correspondence from the Prosecutor, Judge Arbour, on the 3rd of September, 1997, item 10, basically saying, after a long series of events, to Defence Minister Jelavic in so many words, "Look, enough is enough. Produce the documents." That resulted in a letter from Mr. Jelavic in item 11, dated the 18th of December, 1997, in which he committed to produce the documents. And ultimately, on 22nd of October, 1997, some bundle of documents, approximately seven or eight inches thick, were in fact turned over to the Prosecutor's representative in Sarajevo. In reality, Your Honour, and as Mr. Harmon will know from his more direct personal involvement, once again, as has been true in some of the other proceedings that we've been involved in today, the documents produced were, for the most part, non-responsive and irrelevant. There was simply a volume of paper, most of which had no value to the Prosecutor. About that time, Your Honour, then going to item 13, there was some additional applications and orders to the Federation, one on the 17th of December, 1997 and another one in item 17 on the 27th of February, 1998. In response to both of those orders, no documents were produced. In fact, Your Honour, it's safe to say that at this point in time, except for the seven or eight inches worth of documents produced by Mr. Jelavic in October of 1997, in the three years there has been no production of documents at any time by the Bosnian Croat part of the Federation. I say the Bosnian Croat part, Your Honour, because as the Court will understand from our papers and probably has come to understand in the course of these proceedings, the Muslim side of the Federation, if you will, for the most part, is not in a position to have access to many of those documents, given the continuing nature of the division of the entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then in specifically the Kordic case, Your Honour, starting with item 24, was a request for assistance. Not a binding order but initially a Rule 29 request for assistance that went to the Federation. Again with no effect. No documents ever produced at all. That was followed up by -- if you go to item 32, the request for assistance was followed by a binding order on the 25th of January, 1999, which the Court then granted; item 35, which the then Court -- binding order entered by the Court on the 4th of February, 1999. It was that binding order, outstanding order, which led to the compliance hearing last May. The Court ordered at that time -- granted the Prosecutor's application with the exception of paragraphs 28 and 39 and directed the Federation respond by 5th of April of last year. Going to item 38, you will see that, in fact, no documents were produced in compliance with the Court's order, leading to item 39, the Prosecutor then, on the 16th of April, requested a hearing on the Federation's non-compliance. Then going on to item 44, on the 27th of April, this Chamber set a hearing for the 20th of May to allow -- "To allow the BiH representatives to explain why it," that is the Federation, "had not complied with the previous order." That then led to item 46, that on the 20th of May last year, there was, in fact, a compliance hearing for this Chamber that concluded that the Federation was, quote, "in breach of its duty to comply with the 4th February order." That then takes us on to item 49. Following the Court's hearing on May 20th, a written order was issued on the 1st of June. Again, the Court recorded or found the Federation's non-compliance and then entered the following additional order: Ordered the Federation, quote, "to identify specific senior officials, either at the ministerial or at another level, who are responsible for complying with the Trial Court's order and to direct them to comply." In the week or two after, the evidence would show, after that June 1st order, in item 50 the Prime Minister of the Federation indeed, in written orders or written communications, identified the following specific senior officials and ordered them again, having first ordered them to comply as early as February of last year, but ordered again or directed that they comply with the Court's order to -- and those officials being the BiH Federal Minister of Defence, the BiH Federal Minister of Justice, and the BiH Federal Minister of the Interior. Unfortunately, notwithstanding that further direction, still no documents were produced, which then takes us to item 52. On the 22nd of June, the Prosecutor requested a hearing on this matter, which in this respect brings us to today's hearing. At the same time, Your Honour, while that particular series of events was unfolding -- I'll go back to item 34. I must point out, with no particular offence meant toward Mr. Tomic, who joins us today, that even as far back as January of last year, Justice Arbour in our office, having increasing difficulties with getting any cooperation or assistance from the Bosnian Croat side of the Federation, and in a letter to the President of the Federation, Judge Arbour raised her concerns. That letter is a matter of record, attached to our submission. Going to item number 41, and again simultaneous with some of the other events we've now been through, on the 16th of April the Prosecutor applied for a further binding order, a new binding order for a different set of documents, which then takes us to item 48 in the chart. On the 1st of June at the same -- in fact, the same date as the Court's order on the February 4th order, on the 1st of June the Court found the Prosecutor's 16 April application to be specific, relevant, and not unduly onerous, and ordered the Federation to produce the documents by 1 August 1999, which takes us to item 57, and we have to report to the Court that, in fact, no documents were produced, essentially, if you will, setting up, Your Honour, at least a second, if not third or fourth, instance of non-compliance. We then have, after that, one outstanding application dated the 19th of July, which is item 53, and that application is pending. We hope the Court will act on that. That is a very quick review of three years worth of events, the net result of which is, again, except for the handful of irrelevant documents produced by First Minister, now President, Jelavic in October of '97, no documents of any sort being provided to this Tribunal since that time. There are at least two now outstanding orders with non-compliance and one application pending. We would say, Your Honour, that this history is again an instance where these are not isolated incidents. It reflects, once again, a strategy or policy of obstruction, resistance, delay to this Tribunal's work by the Bosnian Croat part of the Federation. I say that because in this particular instance, I should say for the Court, and the Court will hear from the representatives later, we have not, in these respects, had any trouble working with Mr. Ahmic or the Bosniak side. Mr. Ahmic has been entirely cooperative and has tried to assist us as much as he could in these matters. But as I said earlier, the Bosnian Muslim or Bosniak side of the house, if you will, is, generally speaking, not in a position to have access to these -- to what were at one time and perhaps still are HVO or Herceg-Bosna government documents. Again, Your Honour, it's our position that it's not by accident that there has been continuing non-compliance since January 1997 but a policy of resistance to this Tribunal's work. I think, Your Honour, what I want to do is again I'm going to rely more extensively this afternoon than this morning on our papers. There is every reason for the Prosecution and for the Court to conclude that there is, in fact, or at least was -- I guess I should say at least was at one time a substantial volume of relevant material that must have existed. Here again, we know from the investigations conducted by this institution to date that the HVO, Herceg-Bosna, the HDZ political party, these were all modern organisations; yes, perhaps not to English standards, perhaps not to an American standard, but nonetheless very bureaucratically oriented and, in fact, coming out of a communist system in which paper can be extremely important, but there was extensive record keeping. And we've cited in our brief just a few instances on page 3; repeated indication after indication of documents being archived, documents being sent to central records, documents being sent to files, documents being sent to the personnel department. There was extensive record keeping, and there is every reason to believe that those documents at one time existed, at least; further, that an archive was, in fact, established as long ago as 1993. I'm looking now and I'll just touch upon pages 4 and 5 of our submission. I want to highlight one particular document to the Court, if I can, if no others today at least in this part of our submission, and that is what is Exhibit 1 to the Prosecutor's submission, and it's probably worth -- if the Court has access to the exhibits, I think on this one it's worth pausing a moment to look at the actual exhibit. In fact, if the usher has access to it, perhaps he could put it on the ELMO. It would be Exhibit 1 attached to the Prosecutor's 22 December 1999 submission. If it's easier, I can simply hand you one. Yes, that's all right. Maybe just the first two or three pages. For the record, Exhibit 1, for the purposes of this hearing and for the purposes of our December 22nd submission, this is a document titled "Work Log." If you go to the second page, Mr. Usher, the actual decision, this was a document generated or at least being communicated at this time by the chief of the Travnik Defence Administration, Anto Puljic. It's our understanding, Your Honour, based on investigation, that as "Travnik Defence Administration" is used here doesn't mean simply the municipality of Travnik or the town of Travnik but essentially the region known as Central Bosnia, what would have been the province -- the Travnica province under the Vance-Owen Plan, and so it was a regional organisation, if you will, and this is the chief. You can get a sense, Your Honours, from looking at this particular document, the top part of it, just how official this all is. This is no mere happenstance. There's legislation, there's gazettes, there's statutes, there are formal decisions from the Croatian Defence Council. Going to the middle of the page, "a decision on reference numbers of documents at the Travnik Defence Administration," and they even have a coding system. There's even some numbers set aside for recruitment, some for civilian defence, et cetera, et cetera. What's particularly interesting to this particular case is that at the top of the third page, if the usher could go to that, and if you could show the very top right corner, please, if I have the right document. Handwritten on the original Serbo-Croatian version, which is attached, the notation "11 August 1993," and I'm sorry and I don't think there will be any dispute, I'm sure, "Verified for Mr. Kordic's needs." If you look at the body very briefly of the document, you'll see the nature of the document is apparently being communicated to Mr. Kordic, being extensive orders, military records, appointments, assignments, et cetera. I simply stop and emphasise that particular document for a moment again to give the Court some further idea. These documents existed, have existed. Mr. Kordic, as a central figure in Herceg-Bosna and the HVO, was right in the middle of the paper trail. And as the Court has heard the Prosecution say before, there's no reason to believe other than that there were extensive documents that would have passed through Mr. Kordic's hands, if you will, either authored by Mr. Kordic or his staff or being sent to him and his staff. Again, in three years the Bosnian Croat side of the Federation has generated none of those documents, again except for the few in October of 1997. The next few pages talk about an archive, the existence of an archive. We submit, Your Honours, that it was well documented to have existed at least up until 1997, if not later. In paragraph 15, for instance, of our papers, we point out the fact that at least as recently as the 28th of February, 1998, Major-General Ivica Primorac, who, again to follow up again on what Mr. Nice introduced us to a few minutes ago, this is the same Ivica Primorac who was the head of the Bosnian Croat Intelligence Service, was saying in a letter to Deputy Prosecutor Blewett confirming at that time that, in fact, certain HVO documents had been produced to the Office of the Prosecutor from the archivist for the Herceg-Bosna war archive. I'll stop at that, Your Honour, on that particular piece of the picture. The next part of our brief, Your Honour, goes into again this history of non-compliance. In paragraphs 18 through -- excuse me, pages 18 through 27 cover much of the ground that we've covered through the summary chart. Again, simply no compliance. It's rather telling, Your Honours, that it occurred to me that it is not a stretch to say that Ahmici, the incidents in Ahmici, the atrocities there, were one of the events that led to the creation of this Tribunal in 1993. One could point to a handful of particular incidents, certainly Srebrenica, certainly Ahmici, perhaps others, certainly others, that led to the Security Counsel creating the very body that we all find ourselves sitting at this afternoon. It's either ironic or unfortunate that here we are, some seven years later, still trying to obtain basic documents about the Ahmici atrocity. Again, Your Honour, it's the Prosecution position that these things are not by accident but a matter of policy, as a matter of a strategy of continued hostility to this body. We have set that out in some detail in pages 27 through 34 of our submission of the 22nd of December. Again, I'm not going to cover it in any great detail this afternoon, save two points. Part of -- to be extremely candid, Your Honour, and I say this with representatives of the Federation in the courtroom, part of the concerns of the Prosecutor is that we will find ourselves, after all these years, not having been produced any of these documents, only to get into the Defence case in the trial itself of Kordic and Cerkez and find ourselves then confronted with a flood of documents only introduced by the Defence but never available to the Prosecution. To some extent that exact scenario happened in the Blaskic case. And if I can direct the Court, I think it's a point worth pausing on, to paragraph 71, page 33 of our submission. The Court will recall that Colonel Blaskic was on the witness stand himself for some number of weeks, testified in great detail, almost on a minute-by-minute basis of some days what he was doing, what orders he was giving, what communication he was receiving, and, in fact, this was alluded to again, I believe, by Mr. Nice yesterday. In fact, on the 16th of April, there are a substantial number, and I come to the Court unfortunately not with a number firmly in mind, but something in excess of a dozen or so phone calls between Colonel Blaskic and Dario Kordic on the 16th of April. More than 12. By Colonel Blaskic's own testimony, on the date of Ahmici, he's on the telephone with Dario Kordic more than 12 times. This concern that Colonel Blaskic had come in his defence and asked to speak great detail about his records and the Defence was able to produce a number of documents, again never having been shown to the Prosecution until the Defence case, as Mr. Harmon can verify, that is not lost, that situation, the significance of that situation was not lost on the Blaskic Trial Chamber. On 22nd of April, some two or three months before the conclusion of that trial, the Trial Chamber issued an order titled "Order for the production of documents used to prepare for testimony." In the middle of the quote on page 33, to highlight what was driving the Court's concern, the order said, "Considering that in his testimony Blaskic offered such detailed and exhaustive evidence that would be impossible for any witness to do so relying solely on his own memory, that the witness himself asserted that he's relying inter alia on the above-mentioned sources, a diary, a military log, an archive," ordered -- first of all, ordered the Defence to disclose to the Trial Chamber the documents in question -- that is, the war diary and the military log -- by the 15th of May, 1999, and ordered the Federation, same Federation that appears before you this afternoon, ordered the Federation, if necessary, to again submit these same documents to the Court by that date. Continuing on over into paragraph 72. There was some correspondence forthcoming then from the Federation, ironically perhaps, at about the same time this Court was issuing its 1st of June order, where again the Federation produced no documents. And the long and short of it is, Your Honours, the Federation produced no documents in response to Judge Jorda's order either, still, a third, fourth, fifth or sixth instance of non-compliance. Never produced the documents that the Blaskic Chamber ordered. As I've already indicated to the Court and as Mr. Nice has as well, in paragraph 74, it was only some few months ago that this same Mr. Jelavic became the chair of the presidency of the Federation, the position he holds today, a position that he holds at the very same time that the Federation continues to be in repeated non-compliance. The same Mr. Jelavic that Judge McDonald issued a show cause order for contempt in February 1997. So here we are some almost three years later, same Mr. Jelavic, same non-production of documents. I think that's all I'm going to emphasise, Your Honour. Our brief paper on additional aspects in various detail but it speaks well enough for itself. I did prepare, Your Honour, and I think it's worth distributing at this time, two newspaper articles which touch upon a matter already talked about by Mr. Nice, but I see no reason for the Court not to have this information. You may have seen these in the course of your own daily newspaper reading, perhaps, but I think as the Court sees these documents, the full picture of some of the things that have been happening in the past six weeks, certain information that's come to the Prosecutor's attention, will perhaps come together and make more sense. So if I could hand to the usher -- I'm happy to provide them to the representatives of the Federation as well, several copies. We've marked it, for purposes of the record, Your Honour, as Exhibit 8, and just so there is no confusion, there is not, at this juncture, Exhibits 1 through 7, but simply marked a unique number for purposes of the record. The first is an article from the Financial Times dated the 20th of December. The second is an article from the same date from the International Herald Tribune. These detail in part, Your Honour, the actions by SFOR in investigating essentially a Croat/Bosnian Croat intelligence network operating in a false building in Mostar. It was conducted under the -- the investigation was conducted under the Dayton Agreement because of these activities being anti-Dayton. The Court will see, when it has a chance to read the articles in full, if it has not seen these articles before, that it became clear that, in fact, a large measure of this intelligence operation is directed against this Tribunal, to the point of investigators and staff of this Tribunal being surveilled in the field. I submit to the Court this is hardly an indication of good faith cooperation with the Tribunal. That concludes my remarks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, before you finish, there's something I want to raise. In paragraph 82 of your report, you mention what you're asking us to do, and so that the representatives can deal with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- it would be helpful for us to hear what it is you're asking the Trial Chamber to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, this again takes us back to the existing jurisprudence of the Tribunal, which admittedly perhaps is quite limited at this time, based primarily on the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Blaskic subpoena litigation from October of 1997. As perhaps was pointed out this morning, the issues are not simple, I think the intellectually honest answer to some extent, and perhaps my understanding of it that I've operated on, the basis of, is not 100 per cent accurate. It has been our understanding, and the Prosecution has tried to move forward on the premise that were we to get to the point as we were attempting to posture these proceedings last May and June, that in the face of continued non-compliance by the Federation and the Prime Minister's subsequent identification and further direction to the Ministers of Defence, Justice and Interior, to, in fact, comply, and then given their continuing -- or the Federation's continuing non-compliance, it may posture us in a sense that under the logic or reasoning of the judgement that we talked about this morning, that is, the motion that a public official is downgraded, to use the judgement's term, to acting in a private capacity, subjects that person to potentially, at least, direct process from this Court. Now, I'm not going to again stand here and tell the Court that that's all necessarily crystal clear because it probably isn't. All I can say is that I think for all of us, the Prosecution and for the Court, has to find its way through here as best as we all can. There has to be -- I think logic and the implied powers of this institution have to suggest that there is a way for the Court to at least to make further attempts to obtain compliance. In fact, there is certain language in the Blaskic judgement that talks about the implied and inherent powers of this Tribunal. Powers, for instance, reserved under Rule 54 to issue any orders essentially necessary, and I'm paraphrasing in my own words, but essentially necessary to carry out the Tribunal's mandate. Certainly the Security Council could not have meant for this Tribunal to have orders that were unenforceable. Although, one can write law review articles, perhaps, on whether that's the case. That's where we are. We would think, Your Honours, that that's the only way that we'll move forward, either -- the only other alternative is we stop where we are and this Chamber can recommend or refer to the President a finding of non-compliance by the Federation to be reported to the Security Council, a step which has been taken on several other occasions and was taken as recently, not as the result of a Trial Chamber referral, but as the Court knows, in the instance of Croatia, by the referral of the Prosecutor to Judge McDonald last fall, resulting in a report of non-compliance on Croatia to the Security Council. That avenue is open, I think, if the Court, in the face of the Federation's continuing non-compliance, wants to bring that matter to President Jorda's attention. President Jorda can make a further finding of certification and pass that on to the Security Council for action. I guess those are the two alternatives I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's plain, in the first of two you're asking us to order the Federation to comply. If they don't, to subpoena the Ministers of Defence, Justice, and Interior to appear and explain why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. All indications, Your Honour, and these are parts of our submission that I didn't detail this afternoon, the Defence Minister is the most logically responsible official. Where the two armies were, at least on paper, joined together some couple of years ago, and the date's in our papers, where it was no longer, at least again on paper, no longer the HVO army and the Bosnia Muslim army, but then both became part of the Federal Minister of Defence, both of those organisations, if I can use the word, amalgamated into a single unit, a single army under the direction of the Minister of Defence. By that and by legislation, by Bosnian legislation, by -- which specifically made the Minister of Defence responsible for all existing archives both on the Bosniak side and on the Bosnian Croat side. So it's our position, Your Honour, that under the statute, and history, and governmental structure of the Federation at this time, the Minister of Justice is responsible for what once were the HVO records or war archive. Beyond that, Your Honour, as we have indicated before, it's not unusual to think of the Minister of Justice of most countries as having substantial responsibilities for making sure that a country meets its legal obligation to international organisations, and one would think that the Minister of Justice might have something to say to this Tribunal. So I just mention those two particularly. If I could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can you help us about -- is there any change in this situation, because as you mentioned, there is this rotation in the presidency, a new president, Mr. Jelavic, and so is there -- what about the new situation? Because we described the former situation when we have a former president who gave an order to a Minister of Defence and Justice that were not executed. Now we have another situation which can -- we have to adapt to -- to adapt even the legal liaising to the new situation, and perhaps the representatives here of the Federation can help us about what are their positions now, because we knew in the former hearing what was the position. We have, of course, with decision taken at the level of the presidency, an order sent to the Ministers concerned and no reaction. We have just an exchange of letters and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: This is the first question. The second question for me is: What about -- because for the United Nations, the state is Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Federation is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is the state member of the United Nations. So another difficulty here, at least from a legal point of view. Can you also help us concerning this other problem? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll do my best, Your Honour. The Chamber has quickly taken us into some complicated areas, and I don't profess to be a particular expert on the issues but I'll share with the Court as best I can. As far as I know, the only member state of the U.N. is the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is made up, as you recall, of essentially two entities, the Bosnian-Croat Federation being one of the two, which itself is a Federation, if you will, between the Muslim side and the Croat side, and the other entity being the Republika Srpska. So you have entities, and I think under Dayton and I think under even the most recent rule changes, I think some of the Rules were changed in the last plenary for orders not only to states but entities. Certainly the Federation and Republika Srpska are entities, but I think there's only one state, Your Honour. I'll look -- I think that's right. I'm getting confirmation from my colleagues, Your Honour, on that. In terms of the appointment or naming of officials, the Prime Minister, up until this time, hasn't changed. I can't begin to tell you all the nuances of these different positions and how the Prime Minister relates, for instance, to the president. But the Prime Minister of the Federation today is the same Prime Minister who directed the specific senior officials back in June of last year. So we're perhaps assisted by the fact that that Prime Minister is still the same person. I thought perhaps one of the things, Judge Bennouna, you were going to say, and perhaps its still something that we should put on the table, is whether, in fact, given the continuity of Mr. Jelavic's role in these matters going back to 1997, perhaps Mr. Jelavic is one of the people who should come before the Tribunal. After all he was the one who started this back in 1997. So I'll simply put that on the table as well. Just to finish, Your Honours, with -- I was getting various points from my colleagues. On the phone calls between Kordic and Blaskic, just so the record is clear on that I'm told that those were not all on the 16th of April but were between the 16th and 18th of April, a short time, a key time as the Court knows, and a substantial number of telephone traffic between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic. Just so the record is clear. There is also, as indicated in our papers Your Honour, there have been statements to the effect that the HVO archive was never, in fact, transferred to the Federation archive. In trying to touch on these things briefly it may get more complicated but it's in our papers and I mention it again. Mr. Harmon reminds me of it. There are statements from Federation officials to the effect that the HVO archive was, in fact, never transferred to the federal -- to the new Federation archive. There's one final matter, Your Honour, that we need to go into private session just for about two minutes, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do go into private session, so that I can understand the submission, who do you submit, Mr. Scott, that we should address the subpoenas to, if we were minded to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, putting aside this late nomination, if you will, of Mr. Jelavic, I think again it would be the Minister of Justice, and I don't have the names at my fingertips. I'm happy to provide them to the Court. Most of it is in the correspondence which is attached to our submission. But it would be the Minister of Defence, the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, which of the representatives is going to go first? Yes, Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like briefly to inform you of measures taken in connection with the orders received from this Trial Chamber, after which I would present my position regarding the compliance and non-compliance of the two previous orders and also of the third order issued by the Trial Chamber. The scheduling order of this Trial Chamber, in case number IT-95-14/2-T, dated the 15th of February, 1999, are addressed, together with the previous two orders, to the Prime Minister of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Bicakcic. To the President of this Trial Chamber, I sent yesterday the report of the Prime Minister regarding the third order, and allow me now to read that order in its entirety. "Bosnia-Herzegovina. Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Prime Minister." The number of the document, "01-02-318-99." "Sarajevo, 11th January, 2000. Strictly confidential. Very urgent. International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Trial Chamber III."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I don't want to stop you taking any course. It does create problems for the interpreters when letters are read out. This is quite a lengthy document. It may be convenient -- we've got a copy of it -- if you simply summarised it for the record rather than reading it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I just thought it would be better for me to read it, in view of the beginning of this hearing when we learned that Judge Robinson is absent, so it would be perhaps more convenient for him to have the complete report. But in any event, I shall do my best to summarise it, as you have suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson will have a copy, of course, of this. If you would like to summarise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The summary would be that the Prime Minister says that in executing all orders of Trial Chamber III, he has asked those orders to be honoured but that the expected results were not obtained, and he said that the execution on the part of the responsible ministers was not in good faith, to say the least. Also, the Federal Prime Minister extends full support to the positions of the Prosecutor in his confidential report submitted to the Trial Chamber on the 22nd of December, 1999, and the Federal Prime Minister is of the opinion that the report of the Prosecutor correctly -- I'm sorry. The Prime Minister feels that he has done everything in his power to obtain the requested document, and to honour the orders issued to date, and expects this Trial Chamber, in view of the application of the Prosecutor, to take the measures that the Prosecutor referred to in addressing you prior to me. If I may, I would add that it is obvious that all of us who are involved in the execution of the orders of this Trial Chamber, with the aim of establishing the truth and serving justice and assisting this Trial Chamber, are encountering what I would be bold to say as obstruction on the part of certain bodies within the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for how else can we explain that the previous Minister of Justice, Mr. Ignac Dodik, did not respond to the first two orders of this Trial Chamber? And when he did respond, he did so with the clear intention to disorientate not only the Federal Prime Minister but also this Trial Chamber. I should like to remind Your Honours of the Prime Minister's report of the 10th of August, transferred to this Chamber on the 18th of August, and I could quote just a part of that report which says that, in fact, Minister Dodik, instead of acting in accordance with the orders of the Trial Chamber, actually acted in accordance with the requests of the Defence counsel of the accused Cerkez, and the reports he received from competent institutions, submitted them to the Federal Minister as his response to the orders of the Trial Chamber. Let me just quote from the Prime Minister's letter, saying that those reports too that were forwarded to the Trial Chamber, though, they are actually in response to the requests by the Defence counsel of Mr. Mario Cerkez. One might also ask why the Minister of Justice, Mr. Colak, has not responded to the order of this Trial Chamber. Before coming to this hearing, I received a letter from the Deputy Defence Minister, Mr. Sahib Mahmuden [phoen], in which he denies and rejects the letter of the Defence Minister, Mr. Prce, in which the latter says that the documents are in the archives of the main staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to him, because I think that anyone with any knowledge of the circumstances in Bosnia-Herzegovina must know that those documents cannot be found in the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Miroslav Prce, as the Defence Minister, on the basis of our knowledge established so far points to the fact that the document issue can be found within the framework of the Defence Ministry, has repeatedly provided this Trial Chamber with quite contradictory responses. In this case too, in the case of Mr. Miroslav Prce, like the previous Ignac Dodik, the former Justice Minister of the BH Federation, are intended consciously to mislead the Prime Minister and this Honourable Trial Chamber. As evidence of the obstruction of the Croatian cadres in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, allow me briefly to read a letter that was handed to you yesterday from the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Mehmet Zilic, in which he says, and I quote: "Objectively, I was not able to gain possession of the requested documents, in view of the fact that any such documents listed in the annexes were created in the so-called Ministry of the Interior of Herceg-Bosna, because it is a fact that the so-called Herceg-Bosna Ministry of the Interior existed and was operating on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Further on, the Minister says that the documentation of the so-called Ministry of the Interior of Herceg-Bosna requested by the Tribunal is not kept in the archives of the Federal Ministry of the Interior, and finally he informs this Honourable Trial Chamber that all three previous orders that preceded this hearing were submitted to officials from the ranks of the Croatian people in the headquarters of the Federal Ministry of the Interior and the Cantonal Ministry of the Interior, but that they have failed to respond so far or their response was limited to the statement that they failed to gain possession of the requested document. To sum up, the Bosniak part of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina has done everything it could so far to comply with the orders of the Trial Chamber, but objectively we are unable to gain possession of documents which were created or existed within the HVO organisation and the bodies of the so-called Herceg-Bosna, the HDZ, and the Republic of Croatia. I have been mandated to tell this Honourable Trial Chamber today that I fully support the position taken by the Prosecutor, as presented in the report of the 21st of December of this year to this Trial Chamber, and I also support the position upheld today by Mr. Scott in addressing Your Honours in his submissions today, and I support the position that in addition to Mr. Ante Jelavic, that the Ministers of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina representing the Croatian people should be summoned, the people who are responsible for the execution of court orders, as well as those persons that this Honourable Trial Chamber finds to be responsible for non-compliance of Court orders to date. I hope that my distinguished colleague, Mr. Tomic, will certainly have some additional information to provide, because he told us repeatedly that he needed to consult with officials in the Federation. I hope he has had occasion to have those consultations and that he will convey them to you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you move along a bit, because Judge Bennouna is having some difficulty seeing you. Could you move along to the middle so that Judge Bennouna can see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I apologise. I apologise, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me the floor. I wish to pay my respects to the Court, to my learned friends from the Prosecution, and my colleague from the Federation. I also owe an explanation with reference to the question asked by the Prosecution as to my capacity here today. Today I am here as a conventional lawyer, as any other lawyer, and I was requested to stand in for absent Mr. Muselimovic, who was to take up his duties but has not done so yet, and, therefore, I here appear as a lawyer during a particular session. And after that, I shall ask Mr. Usher to show the authorisation issued by Andric Luzanski, the Vice-President of the Federation of BH. I was somewhat caught aback by a factor which prevents me from answering some allegations in more detail. Namely, it was only after I arrived in The Hague that I learned that the confidential report, that is, the latest submission of the Prosecution, was sent in turn to the Federation of BH but that it was only on the 11th of this month that it was forwarded to Mostar, where I or, rather, Mr. Muselimovic are normally. So this was due to technical reasons which did not depend on me, and I therefore cannot really pronounce myself on all these details. However, out of respect for the Court and my learned friends, I'm not seeking any delay. All I wish to point out is that according to the instructions I was issued and information I received in contact with Croat officials in the Federation of BH, the reasons for non-submission of documentation were already -- that you were already notified about the reasons; that a number of them are lost or mislaid, that some have been misappropriated, because we see some memoirs appearing today without any historical distance, and so on and so forth. But I otherwise feel it is my duty to touch upon two conclusions of the Prosecution, that it is a systematic obstruction and, secondly, an absence of good faith. I think that these conclusions are much too harsh. The Croat side has been pointed out for a long time, and I believe this is an extenuating circumstance rather than as an excuse, that the cooperation with the Tribunal has an inherent component, and that is respect for the interests of all parties. A while ago, we heard an example of misunderstanding, that is, the impossibility of the Croat side to prove some very clear facts which should not really need to be proven under Rule 94, but now the representative of the Prosecution said that the only state member of the United Nations is the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, gentlemen, this is absolutely incorrect, and this error would not be so important but it is reflecting a situation which seems to have prevailed here for years; that is, if the Croat side is objected against because of the absence of good faith, then the Bosniak side evidently is guilty of showing absolutely no flexibility with regard to Croat objections. And therefore my proposal is, first, that the Tribunal -- that the Court should consider the documentation which I attached to my submission and which, in point of fact, covers the Official Gazettes, because I believe that an analysis of that documentation could allow you to draw some important conclusions as regards the fundamental premise on which the document is based, and that would automatically lead to the decrease in the number of requested documentation. That is, one of our objections is having been accused that we are not acting in good faith. Now, we are saying that the question that arises is not good faith but whether small people can survive this Court in any way. If we are mentioning the Security Council, well, the intention of the Security Council was not to conduct proceedings only for Croat crimes without conducting proceedings for crimes against Croats, and I think that some conclusions are beyond time and space. In the former Yugoslavia, we were not allowed and generations were not allowed to mention that during World War II there was a civil war, and we had to learn how we had defeated Germans. So one of our postulates is that if the Court considered the objection that a temporary criminal -- a civil war was raging, that that particular fact would lead it to a completely different point of view and, therefore, requests for completely different documentation or, rather, a decrease in the number and scope of documentation requested. Four; if I look at this objection, that is, the absence of good faith which is addressed to us, I need to emphatically reject that objection. I am not against the proposal that some of the named officials be called again to be given a new deadline, but such qualifications concerning good faith, obstruction, or as my learned friend said, incestuous behaviour, I think that is much too harsh, I should dare say, because nobody has heeded to our objections for years. That is, we, the Croats, cannot prove an elementary fact, that from the Official Gazette it transpires that a particular institution is called this or that. Our objection is that we cannot agree as to what is the army of BH, just as we cannot discuss what is north or south or various chemical formula, and that creates a feeling of impotence. We are a small people and we cannot survive this Tribunal, because some categorical definitions are imposed on us and thereby collective guilt is imposed on us by the selection of days, by the selection of events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I'm not going to allow you to make --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I have concluded, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Anything more you want to say about the application which is made by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only two things I would respectfully invite you to consider, particularly in light of the fact that Mr. Tomic is here simply as a lawyer and not in any other sense as a representative of the Bosnian Croat side of the Federation. Any orders that might be made should, in our respectful submission, be directed directly to the named and post-holding individuals, if the names and posts and addresses are known, but for good order it might be thought prudent to send copies of the orders to both parts of the Federation to ensure that there is no argument in due course that people weren't identified and served. Supplementary to that, might I respectfully suggest, and I should have mentioned this this morning, that any orders that the Chamber may decide to make requesting people to attend to give an account of documents will be most effective if the person concerned is under a duty to provide, in advance, a statement of proof or a summary of what his or her position is on the documents, category by category, with whether there are any such documents existing, if they've been destroyed, to whom they've been transferred, or why they are not being produced, because otherwise it will simply be everything will be coming fresh and it will take a long time for us to analyse it, work it out, and to know whether we accept the evidence that's been given or whether extensive cross-examination would be invited, if we are allowed to cross-examine, or through the Court. So I would simply invite consideration be given to those matters. Sorry for not having mentioned it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you're still standing, Mr. Nice, we are facing the following situation: You are asking us that we address ourselves to the Prime Minister of an entity -- let us call it that, as Mr. Scott did, an entity, very well -- and then this Prime Minister, as Mr. Ahmic has just told us and as we see from the documents, this Prime Minister will write to his Ministers, telling them to carry out the orders from the Tribunal. Those Ministers will answer that they have nothing to implement, that they are not implementing them, or that there are no documents. In any event, two out of three have answered, I think, the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Justice, and the third provided no response. So I can't remember who that was. And now you're asking us -- the Prime Minister has been relieved of further action because he's saying he has nothing, so now we only can address those individuals directly. Perhaps it is better to address God than them. But we would like to -- it is better to address the Saint than God. In any case, you have told us to address ourselves directly to these people. And according to the Blaskic jurisprudence, they can be subpoenaed directly because they failed to obey their government and they become private individuals. And you are telling us now that before telling them to come you told us they needed to be subpoenaed to come and provide explanations, and you're also telling us that perhaps we should ask them to provide written submissions. My question is the following: Before going on to the subpoena, that is an order asking them to come under penalty of sanctions, would it not be an order -- a simple order of the Chamber which we can address to them to come to provide an explanation here without adding a subpoena, because a subpoena would mean that they did not comply with a previous order, an ordinary order, let me call it, an ordinary decision addressed to them. So that is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think we would challenge the appropriateness of seeking their compliance by attendance and/or by a written submission in advance of attendance by an order in the first place, no, rather than expressing it as a subpoena. And I think if I may respectfully say so, Your Honours, an analysis of the steps before an order with a penalty immediately consequent on breach, your analysis of the appropriate steps may well be correct. But in any event, one way or another, if the individuals concerned are minded to comply and obey, then the order will be effective. If they decline to comply with the order, then it won't be long before we'll be seeking a subpoena, and everything's going to have to be -- in light of the time scale, everything will have to be kept in hand, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider these matters. We shall give our judgement or, rather, make an order when Judge Robinson has returned and we are fully composed as a Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.15 p.m. 25
